questions.question: A 32-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, delivers a healthy infant vaginally at 38 weeks' gestation. She had no prenatal care. Both previous deliveries were by cesarean section. After delivery the placenta does not separate, and she rapidly loses 2 L of blood. An emergency hysterectomy is performed. Microscopy of the uterus shows chorionic villi lying directly against myometrial smooth muscle fibers. Which of the following abnormalities of implantation best explains this finding?

answers.A: Absent decidua basalis at the implantation site
answers.B: Implantation low in the endometrial cavity
answers.C: Loss of blood supply to the decidua capsularis
answers.D: Persistent smooth muscle in decidual spiral arteries
answers.E: Premature fusion of capsularis and parietalis

explanations.A: Correct. Placenta accreta spectrum occurs when the blastocyst implants where there is no decidua basalis, typically over a uterine scar, so villi attach to smooth muscle and the placenta cannot separate.
explanations.B: Low implantation produces placenta previa, which presents with painless antepartum bleeding, not failure of placental separation with villi on myometrium.
explanations.C: The decidua capsularis normally loses its blood supply as the embryo grows and fuses with the parietalis; this is not pathologic.
explanations.D: Retained smooth muscle in spiral arteries is normal in the decidua parietalis and does not cause villi to adhere to myometrium.
explanations.E: Fusion of the capsularis and parietalis into the decidua vera is a normal event that obliterates the uterine cavity by 14 to 16 weeks.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 33 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department because of bright red vaginal bleeding that began while she was watching television. She has no abdominal pain or contractions, and the uterus is soft and nontender. Fetal heart tracing is reassuring. Transabdominal ultrasound shows placental tissue completely covering the internal cervical os. Which of the following best explains the position of this placenta?

answers.A: Absence of decidua basalis beneath the blastocyst
answers.B: Excessive extravillous trophoblast invasion
answers.C: Implantation of the blastocyst low in the uterine cavity
answers.D: Increased villous branching from uteroplacental insufficiency
answers.E: Separation of the placenta from the decidua basalis

explanations.A: Implantation without decidua basalis causes placenta accreta spectrum, which presents with failed placental separation after delivery rather than painless antepartum bleeding.
explanations.B: Deep trophoblast invasion relates to abnormal adherence (accreta spectrum), not to where in the cavity the placenta sits.
explanations.C: Correct. Placenta previa results from low implantation, so placenta covers the internal os and bleeds painlessly as the cervix changes.
explanations.D: Increased villous branching is a compensatory change in uteroplacental insufficiency and does not determine placental location.
explanations.E: Premature placental separation (abruption) is typically painful, with a tender, firm uterus, unlike this presentation.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman at 31 weeks' gestation has taken ibuprofen 800 mg three times daily for the past 2 weeks for low back pain. Routine ultrasound shows a dilated fetal right ventricle with tricuspid regurgitation and signs of fetal heart failure. Amniotic fluid volume is normal. Which of the following fetal structures has most likely been affected by this medication?

answers.A: Ductus arteriosus
answers.B: Ductus venosus
answers.E: Umbilical vein

explanations.A: Correct. NSAIDs taken in pregnancy can close the ductus arteriosus prematurely, so right ventricular output can no longer bypass the high-resistance fetal lungs, causing right heart strain.
explanations.B: The ductus venosus carries oxygenated umbilical venous blood past the liver to the IVC; NSAIDs do not close it and its loss would not specifically overload the right ventricle.
explanations.C: The foramen ovale shunts blood from the right to the left atrium and is not prostaglandin dependent, so NSAIDs do not close it.
explanations.D: The umbilical arteries return deoxygenated blood to the placenta; NSAIDs do not constrict them.
explanations.E: The umbilical vein returns oxygenated blood from the placenta; it is not the prostaglandin-dependent fetal shunt.

questions.question: A term male newborn is delivered by uncomplicated vaginal birth. Within seconds he cries vigorously and his lungs expand with air. Over the next minutes, his oxygen saturation rises from 60% to 92%, and echocardiography shows a marked increase in blood flow through the pulmonary arteries. Which of the following changes is most responsible for redirecting right heart output to the lungs?

answers.A: Closure of the ductus venosus by prostaglandins
answers.B: Constriction of pulmonary arterioles by oxygen
answers.C: Decreased systemic resistance after cord clamping
answers.E: Rise in right atrial pressure above left atrial pressure

explanations.A: Prostaglandins keep the ductus arteriosus open; the ductus venosus constricts after birth and does not direct right ventricular output.
explanations.B: Oxygen dilates rather than constricts pulmonary arterioles; constriction would reduce, not increase, pulmonary flow.
explanations.C: Removing the low-resistance placental circuit increases, rather than decreases, systemic vascular resistance.
explanations.D: Correct. Lung expansion and rising oxygen dilate pulmonary arterioles, lowering pulmonary resistance so right heart blood flows to the lungs and the fetal shunts close.
explanations.E: After birth, left atrial pressure rises above right atrial pressure, which closes the foramen ovale; a rise in right atrial pressure would favor right-to-left shunting.

questions.question: A fetal medicine specialist performs a research study measuring oxygen saturation at several points in the circulation of a healthy fetus at 30 weeks' gestation. The placenta and umbilical cord are normal. Blood from which of the following sites is expected to have the highest oxygen saturation?

answers.A: Descending aorta
answers.B: Ductus arteriosus
answers.E: Umbilical artery

explanations.A: The descending aorta receives deoxygenated right ventricular blood via the ductus arteriosus, so its saturation is lower.
explanations.B: The ductus arteriosus carries mostly superior vena cava and right ventricular blood, which is among the least oxygenated in the fetus.
explanations.C: Correct. The ductus venosus carries richly oxygenated blood straight from the umbilical vein before it mixes with deoxygenated IVC blood.
explanations.D: The pulmonary artery carries right ventricular output, made largely of deoxygenated venous return.
explanations.E: The umbilical arteries return deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta, so their saturation is low.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man undergoes laparoscopic cholecystectomy. While retracting the liver, the surgeon points out a fibrous cord running in a fissure on the visceral surface of the liver between the caudate lobe and the left lobe, connecting the left portal vein region to the inferior vena cava. This structure is the remnant of a fetal vessel that carried which of the following?

answers.A: Blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta
answers.B: Blood from the right atrium to the left atrium
answers.C: Deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta
answers.D: Oxygenated blood from the placenta into the liver
answers.E: Oxygenated blood past the liver to the vena cava

explanations.A: That is the ductus arteriosus, which becomes the ligamentum arteriosum, not a ligament of the liver.
explanations.B: That is the foramen ovale, which becomes the fossa ovalis in the interatrial septum.
explanations.C: That is the umbilical arteries, which become the umbilical ligaments on the anterior abdominal wall.
explanations.D: That describes the umbilical vein, which becomes the ligamentum teres in the falciform ligament, not the cord between caudate and left lobes.
explanations.E: Correct. The ligamentum venosum is the remnant of the ductus venosus, which shunted oxygenated umbilical venous blood from the portal circulation to the IVC.

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 22 weeks' gestation has an ultrasound showing a hydropic fetus with cardiomegaly, ascites and an elevated middle cerebral artery peak velocity indicating severe fetal anemia. She and her partner are both of Southeast Asian descent and both have mild microcytic anemia with normal iron studies and normal hemoglobin electrophoresis. Her first child has sickle cell disease and was well until 6 months of age. Which of the following best explains why this fetus is severely affected in utero?

answers.A: Fetal hematopoiesis occurs in the bone marrow
answers.B: Fetal hemoglobin has a lower affinity for oxygen
answers.D: Fetal hemoglobin requires alpha globin chains
answers.E: Fetal hemoglobin requires beta globin chains

explanations.A: During the second trimester, hematopoiesis occurs mainly in the fetal liver; bone marrow takes over in the third trimester.
explanations.B: Fetal hemoglobin has a higher, not lower, oxygen affinity than adult hemoglobin, which helps placental oxygen uptake.
explanations.C: Fetal hemoglobin is composed of 2 alpha and 2 gamma chains, so it does contain gamma chains.
explanations.D: Correct. HbF is alpha2-gamma2, so loss of all alpha chains (Hb Barts disease) prevents functional hemoglobin in utero and causes fetal anemia, heart failure and hydrops.
explanations.E: Fetal hemoglobin has no beta chains, which is why beta-chain disorders such as the sibling's sickle cell disease do not cause anemia in utero.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation asks how her fetus can obtain enough oxygen when the partial pressure of oxygen in the intervillous space is much lower than in her arteries. The physician shows her oxygen dissociation data for maternal and fetal blood. Which of the following best explains how fetal blood takes up oxygen at this low partial pressure?

answers.A: Direct mixing of maternal and fetal blood
answers.B: Higher oxygen affinity of fetal hemoglobin
answers.C: Higher pulmonary blood flow in the fetus
answers.D: Lower fetal 2,3-BPG production by the placenta
answers.E: Rightward shift of the fetal dissociation curve

explanations.A: Maternal and fetal blood do not mix directly; they are separated by a thin syncytiotrophoblast layer.
explanations.B: Correct. Fetal hemoglobin (alpha2-gamma2) has a higher oxygen affinity than adult hemoglobin (lower P50), so it loads oxygen at the low PO2 of the intervillous space.
explanations.C: The fetal lungs receive only about 8% of cardiac output and are not the site of oxygenation.
explanations.D: The placenta does not regulate fetal 2,3-BPG; the higher affinity results from the gamma chains of fetal hemoglobin.
explanations.E: A rightward shift would lower oxygen affinity; fetal blood is shifted to the left.

questions.question: A 4-day-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of oozing blood from his umbilical stump and blood in his stool. He was born at home at term to a 24-year-old woman, and his parents declined all newborn injections. He is exclusively breastfed. He appears well apart from the bleeding. Laboratory studies are shown. A deficiency of which of the following is most likely responsible for these findings?

answers.A: Factor VIII alone
answers.B: Factors II, VII, IX and X
answers.E: Von Willebrand factor multimers

explanations.A: Isolated factor VIII deficiency (hemophilia A) prolongs the PTT but not the PT.
explanations.B: Correct. Fetal and neonatal levels of vitamin K-dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X, protein C and S) are low and fall after birth; without vitamin K prophylaxis this causes bleeding with a prolonged PT.
explanations.C: Fibrinogen is normal here, and isolated hypofibrinogenemia would not be prevented by vitamin K.
explanations.D: The platelet count is normal, so thrombocytopenia does not explain the bleeding.
explanations.E: Von Willebrand disease causes mucocutaneous bleeding with a normal PT and is not related to omitted newborn prophylaxis.

questions.question: A male infant is born at 28 weeks' gestation to a 31-year-old woman whose membranes ruptured prematurely. At 3 weeks of age he develops late-onset sepsis. His mother was fully vaccinated, and serum IgG in a term infant born the same week is markedly higher than in this infant. Which of the following best explains this infant's low serum IgG concentration?

answers.A: Breast milk lacks the IgA needed to protect him
answers.B: Fetal B cells cannot produce any immunoglobulin
answers.C: IgM rather than IgG crosses the placenta
answers.D: Maternal IgG cannot cross the placenta before term
answers.E: Most maternal IgG crosses in the last 4 weeks

explanations.A: Maternal IgA in breast milk gives mucosal protection in the gut but does not determine serum IgG levels.
explanations.B: Fetuses can mount antibody responses to in-utero infection, but almost all fetal immunoglobulin normally comes from the mother.
explanations.C: IgG is the immunoglobulin that crosses the placenta; IgM does not.
explanations.D: Transplacental IgG transfer begins at 16 weeks, so some IgG crosses well before term.
explanations.E: Correct. Transplacental IgG transfer starts at 16 weeks but is greatest in the last 4 weeks of pregnancy, so preterm infants are relatively immunosuppressed.

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation comes to labor and delivery with regular painful contractions. Her cervix is 4 cm dilated. She is given intramuscular betamethasone, two doses 24 hours apart, before delivering 3 days later. The neonate requires only brief supplemental oxygen. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which this treatment benefited the neonate?

answers.A: Accelerated closure of the ductus arteriosus
answers.B: Faster maturation of fetal hemoglobin to HbA
answers.E: Reduced pulmonary vascular resistance in utero

explanations.A: Glucocorticoids are not used to close the ductus; NSAIDs, not steroids, cause ductal closure.
explanations.B: The switch from HbF to HbA is not driven by antenatal steroids and does not prevent respiratory distress.
explanations.C: Alveolar septation and multiplication occur in the alveolar phase, which continues until about 8 years of age, and is not the steroid effect.
explanations.D: Correct. Maternal glucocorticoids increase surfactant production by type 2 pneumocytes, lowering the risk and severity of respiratory distress syndrome.
explanations.E: Pulmonary vascular resistance falls at birth with lung expansion and oxygen; this is not how antenatal steroids help.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman, gravida 1, has a routine ultrasound at 20 weeks' gestation showing no amniotic fluid and no visible fetal kidneys or bladder. An ultrasound at 11 weeks' gestation for dating had shown a normal amount of amniotic fluid. Which of the following best explains the normal amniotic fluid volume at 11 weeks?

answers.A: Fetal swallowing had not yet begun
answers.B: Fetal urine is concentrated in the first trimester
answers.C: Fetal urine production begins at about 12 weeks
answers.D: The mesonephros produces most early amniotic fluid
answers.E: The urogenital sinus secretes early amniotic fluid

explanations.A: Fetal swallowing removes amniotic fluid; a lack of swallowing would increase fluid but does not explain normal early volume with absent kidneys.
explanations.B: Fetal kidneys cannot concentrate urine at any stage of gestation.
explanations.C: Correct. Fetal urine production starts at about 12 weeks and dominates amniotic fluid only by the mid second trimester, so fluid can be normal in the first trimester even with renal agenesis.
explanations.D: Amniotic fluid is not mainly mesonephric urine; fetal urine production begins at about 12 weeks.
explanations.E: The urogenital sinus gives rise to the bladder and urethra and does not secrete amniotic fluid.

questions.question: A 22-year-old woman at 18 weeks' gestation has prelabor rupture of membranes confirmed by sterile speculum examination. Over the following weeks, ultrasound shows persistent anhydramnios. She chooses to continue the pregnancy, and the infant is born at 32 weeks with severe respiratory failure, flattened facial features and contractures of the limbs. Disruption of which of the following stages of lung development most directly explains this infant's respiratory failure?

answers.A: Alveolar
answers.B: Canalicular
answers.E: Saccular

explanations.A: The alveolar phase, with septation and multiplication of alveoli, occurs mostly after birth.
explanations.B: Correct. In the canalicular phase (about 17 to 27 weeks), amniotic fluid is needed to circulate lamellar bodies and surfactant into the developing alveoli; anhydramnios here causes lung hypoplasia (Potter sequence).
explanations.C: The embryonic phase forms the trachea and main bronchi early in gestation, before amniotic fluid plays its key role.
explanations.D: The pseudoglandular phase forms the terminal bronchioles before 17 weeks, before membrane rupture in this patient.
explanations.E: The saccular phase forms gas exchange units late in pregnancy; the critical dependence on amniotic fluid is earlier, in the canalicular phase.

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation is found to have a fundal height of 36 cm. Ultrasound shows an amniotic fluid index of 32 cm and the fetal abdominal image shown. Earlier cell-free DNA screening was high risk for trisomy 21. Which of the following best explains the increased amniotic fluid volume?

answers.A: Excess fetal urine from osmotic diuresis
answers.B: Failure of the fetus to swallow from neuromuscular disease
answers.C: Impaired fluid passage through the fetal duodenum
answers.E: Leak of fluid across a renal outflow obstruction

explanations.A: Osmotic diuresis from fetal hyperglycemia can increase fluid, but the image shows a GI obstruction.
explanations.B: Impaired swallowing from neuromuscular disease can cause polyhydramnios, but this fetus has an obstruction seen on ultrasound.
explanations.C: Correct. The double bubble sign of duodenal atresia, associated with trisomy 21, shows obstruction that prevents swallowed fluid from being absorbed and returned via the GU tract, causing polyhydramnios.
explanations.D: Lung fluid contributes little to amniotic volume and is not related to this image.
explanations.E: Urinary outflow obstruction reduces, not increases, amniotic fluid.

questions.question: A male newborn is jittery and feeding poorly 2 hours after birth at 38 weeks' gestation. He weighs 4,600 g. His mother has type 1 diabetes with poor glycemic control throughout pregnancy. Laboratory studies are shown. Which of the following best explains this newborn's hypoglycemia?

answers.A: Deficient fetal glycogen stores
answers.B: Immature fetal pancreatic insulin secretion
answers.E: Placental lactogen excess in the newborn

explanations.A: This large infant has ample glycogen stores; the problem is excess insulin, not lack of fuel.
explanations.B: The fetal pancreas produces insulin in response to hyperglycemia; here production is excessive, not immature.
explanations.C: Maternal insulin does not cross the placenta in a meaningful amount; the hyperinsulinemia is the fetus's own.
explanations.D: Correct. Glucose crosses the placenta freely, so maternal hyperglycemia drives excess fetal insulin production, which persists after the maternal glucose supply ends at birth.
explanations.E: Human placental lactogen raises maternal insulin resistance and is cleared after delivery; it does not cause neonatal hypoglycemia.

questions.question: A 31-year-old woman at 16 weeks' gestation has second-trimester serum screening. Ultrasound shows a structurally normal male fetus with normal growth. She has no signs of virilization. Results are shown. At age 3 months the infant develops dark, scaly skin on the trunk and extensor limbs. Which of the following best explains the low estrogen level on the screen?

answers.A: 21-hydroxylase deficiency in the fetus
answers.B: Aromatase deficiency in the placenta
answers.E: Uteroplacental insufficiency

explanations.A: Fetal 21-hydroxylase deficiency increases fetal androgen precursors, which would raise, not lower, placental estrogen synthesis.
explanations.B: Placental aromatase deficiency lowers estrogen but causes maternal virilization from accumulating androgens, which is absent here.
explanations.C: Correct. Placental estrogen depends on fetal DHEA-S, which the placenta must desulfate; sulfatase deficiency (X-linked, with later ichthyosis in boys) causes low maternal estrogen.
explanations.D: Trisomy 18 can lower estrogen, but it also lowers AFP and hCG and causes structural anomalies and growth restriction, which are absent.
explanations.E: Uteroplacental insufficiency would typically cause fetal growth restriction, and growth here is normal.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 16 weeks' gestation is counseled because her first child was born spontaneously at 31 weeks. Her cervix is long and closed. She is started on weekly progesterone injections, which are continued until 36 weeks. Which of the following best describes the intended effect of this therapy?

answers.A: Increasing fetal surfactant production
answers.B: Maintaining the corpus luteum
answers.E: Stimulating cervical ripening

explanations.A: Surfactant production is increased by maternal glucocorticoids given when preterm delivery is imminent, not by progesterone.
explanations.B: The corpus luteum is maintained by hCG in early pregnancy; this is not the purpose of progesterone in the second trimester.
explanations.C: Correct. Progesterone maintains uterine quiescence, and functional progesterone withdrawal is thought to precipitate labor; supplementation lowers preterm birth risk in at-risk patients.
explanations.D: Fetal adrenal DHEA-S is the precursor for placental estrogen; progesterone therapy is not given to change it.
explanations.E: Cervical ripening accompanies labor; progesterone is given to prevent, not promote, it.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman at 6 weeks' gestation undergoes emergency laparoscopy for ovarian torsion. Her serum progesterone falls sharply after removal of a large cystic structure from the left ovary, and she is started on progesterone supplementation to prevent pregnancy loss. Which of the following hormones normally sustains the structure that was removed?

answers.A: Estradiol
answers.B: Human chorionic gonadotropin
answers.E: Progesterone

explanations.A: Estradiol stimulates follicle development and endometrial proliferation; it does not maintain the corpus luteum.
explanations.B: Correct. hCG, made in greatest amounts in the first trimester and structurally similar to LH, maintains the corpus luteum so it keeps secreting progesterone until the placenta takes over.
explanations.C: Human placental lactogen increases maternal insulin resistance; it does not support the corpus luteum.
explanations.D: Inhibin from the placenta may inhibit FSH-mediated ovulation and regulate hCG synthesis but does not maintain the corpus luteum.
explanations.E: Progesterone is the product of the corpus luteum, not the hormone that sustains it.

questions.question: A 36-year-old woman with chronic hypertension at 33 weeks' gestation has a fundal height of 28 cm. Ultrasound shows normal fetal anatomy and reduced amniotic fluid. First-trimester cell-free DNA screening was low risk, and she has no history of infection or tobacco use. Results are shown. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?

answers.A: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection
answers.B: Constitutionally small fetus
answers.E: Placental insufficiency from hypertension

explanations.A: Congenital infection typically causes symmetric growth restriction, often with ultrasound findings such as calcifications, which are absent.
explanations.B: A constitutionally small fetus is proportionately small with normal fluid, not one with a small abdomen, normal head and low fluid.
explanations.C: Aneuploidy tends to cause early, symmetric restriction often with anomalies; anatomy is normal and screening was low risk.
explanations.D: Fetal hyperinsulinemia from maternal hyperglycemia causes macrosomia, not a small abdominal circumference.
explanations.E: Correct. Maternal hypertension causes placental insufficiency, producing late, asymmetric growth restriction in which the head is spared and abdominal circumference falls below the 10th percentile.

questions.question: A male infant is born at 30 weeks' gestation after spontaneous preterm labor. He is appropriately grown for his gestational age. On examination he has thin, translucent skin, very little subcutaneous fat, and his blood glucose falls to 35 mg/dL in the first hours despite normal insulin levels. Which of the following best explains his limited fat and glycogen reserves?

answers.A: Fat and glycogen accrue mainly after 32 weeks
answers.B: Fetal growth before 32 weeks is mainly by hypertrophy
answers.C: Fetal growth is fastest in the second trimester
answers.D: Hyperplasia ends at 16 weeks of gestation
answers.E: Placental lactogen is absent before 32 weeks

explanations.A: Correct. After 32 weeks fetal growth is by hypertrophy at 30 to 35 g/day, the period when most fetal fat and glycogen accumulate, so this infant missed it.
explanations.B: Hypertrophy alone is the pattern after 32 weeks; between 16 and 32 weeks growth is by both hyperplasia and hypertrophy.
explanations.C: Fetal growth is fastest in the third trimester, at about 30 to 35 g/day after 32 weeks.
explanations.D: Hyperplasia continues alongside hypertrophy from 16 to 32 weeks; it does not end at 16 weeks.
explanations.E: Human placental lactogen alters maternal metabolism throughout pregnancy; its absence is not why this infant lacks stores.
